title: Markandeya and the flood
word: reading the Isha in the original
hookLine: a sage watches the whole world sink and finds a baby on a leaf
carry: all that's born falls apart; the deathless doesn't
tomorrow: what did Death offer a boy to stop asking?

lines: A BABY ON A BANYAN LEAF.
cards: The sage Markandeya has been blessed with a very long life, and he asks the Lord for one more thing: let me see your maya, the power that makes the world. The Bhagavata tells what he gets.
The sky darkens, the rain comes, the oceans rise, and the whole world goes under. Markandeya swims alone for what feels like ages, in a flood with no shore. Then, on the water, a banyan tree.
On one of its leaves, a baby, dark and glowing, calmly sucking his own toe. Markandeya comes close, and with one breath the baby draws him in.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD, INSIDE A CHILD.
teach.b: Inside the child, Markandeya sees everything: mountains, oceans, cities, his own hermitage. The baby breathes out, and he's back on the water. Then the flood is gone, and he's sitting at home.
Hindus have long taught that worlds come into being and dissolve, again and again: creation, and pralaya, the great dissolution. And through all of it, something doesn't dissolve.
Markandeya saw it: a child on a leaf, unworried, holding the whole world. Now Isha twelve to fourteen. They echo the three verses before, with new words.
And in verse fourteen, vinasha: destruction, falling apart. Whoever knows coming-into-being and falling-apart, both, together, crosses death by one and reaches the deathless by the other.
Readers explain the pair differently. But the shape is plain: don't look only at things being born, or only at things breaking. Know both, and know what neither touches.
The Bhagavad Gita puts it bluntly: jatasya hi dhruvo mrityuh.

teach.h: FOR THE BORN, DEATH IS CERTAIN.
teach.b: For the born, death is certain. In Hindu teaching that isn't gloom. It's the ground of the calm Markandeya found in the middle of a flood.

how: Markandeya's vision of the child on the banyan leaf is a favorite in Hindu art and storytelling; many families give old or broken murtis back to a river with respect, rather than throwing them away.

games.q: what does “reading the isha in the original” mean?
o: reading the Isha as a song with a fixed chorus
reading the Isha's verses twice to memorize them
reading the Isha's own words: becoming and falling apart, known together

games.q: the flood and the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the sage who saw the flood
the great dissolution of a world

s: verses twelve to fourteen just repeat nine to eleven
the frame echoes, with new words: sambhuti, becoming, and vinasha, falling apart.
in the Bhagavata, Markandeya sees the whole world inside a baby on a banyan leaf
drawn in by the child's breath, then breathed out onto the water.
in Hindu teaching, the end of a world is the end of everything
worlds come and go in cycles; the deathless doesn't.

games.q: Nani's temple is being rebuilt, and an old, chipped murti will be given back to the river. a cousin is upset it's being 'thrown away.' what fits this week's teaching?
o: what's made comes and goes; Hindus give old forms back with respect, and the Lord isn't lost.
it's a disaster; a chipped form means the god is gone.
nothing physical matters at all, so it doesn't matter how it's done.
games.why: know both together: the form came into being and will fall apart, and what it pointed to doesn't. that's why the giving back is done with care.

practice: Say one line out loud, softly, three times. If you pray, the Gita's: jatasya hi dhruvo mrityuh, for the born, death is certain. If you don't, simply: everything that begins, ends.
Each time, notice what's still here while you say it: the breath, the listening. Then sit with that.

wordCard.voice: Reading the Isha in the original, verses twelve to fourteen: sambhuti, becoming, and vinasha, falling apart. Know both, together.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: vinasha, destruction, falling apart, the new word in Isha 14.

carryVoice: Your line: all that's born falls apart; the deathless doesn't. Markandeya saw it on a leaf. That's today.

sources.ref: Isha Upanishad 12, first line (andham tamah pravishanti ye 'sambhutim upasate)
Isha Upanishad 13 (from becoming, from not-becoming; iti shushruma dhiranam)
Isha Upanishad 14 (sambhutim ca vinasham ca; vinashena mrityum tirtva sambhutyamritam ashnute)
Bhagavata Purana 12.8–12.9 (Markandeya asks to see the Lord's maya; the flood; the child on the banyan leaf; drawn in by his breath, he sees the worlds inside)
Bhagavad Gita 2.27 (jatasya hi dhruvo mrityur dhruvam janma mritasya ca)
